Tests of provider effects

Source: vignettes/testing.Rmd
testing.Rmd

Profiling reduces to one hypothesis test per provider, of the null that the provider’s effect equals a reference effect \(\gamma_0\), the median of the provider effects. Three difficulties shape the test: small providers, some with outcomes that are all identical; observations correlated within patient; and a reference distribution that may not describe how providers ordinarily vary. They correspond to three choices, made independently: the statistic, its variance and the reference distribution. This page covers the first two; the third is Reference distributions.

The taxonomy

naive (working independence) robust (patient-clustered sandwich) stabilized robust (pooled correlation)
Wald \(Z_W\) \(Z_{RW}\) \(Z_{SRW}\)
score \(Z_S\) \(Z_{RS}\) \(Z_{SRS}\)
exact \(Z_E\)

Three statistics. A Wald statistic compares the estimated effect with the reference, scaled by its standard error; it needs the estimate to exist, and at a provider whose outcomes are all identical it does not. A score statistic evaluates the estimating function at the null, so nothing is estimated for the provider under test and it is finite exactly where the Wald statistic breaks. An exact test uses the finite-sample distribution of the provider’s total under the null: Poisson-binomial for a binary outcome, from which a mid-p value and an interval follow; it assumes the observations within the provider are independent.

Three variances. The naive variance treats a patient’s repeated observations as independent, which they are not, so it is too small. The robust variance is the patient-clustered sandwich, consistent whatever the correlation, but at small providers it is variable and biased downward, so the robust test flags too many small providers. The stabilized variance (Pan 2001) replaces the provider’s own estimate of the within-patient correlation with one pooled over every patient in the data with the same number of observations: the correlation is a feature of the outcome rather than of the provider, so this is a natural thing to borrow, and the estimator is far less variable at small providers.

test() 

library(pprof)
d <- sim_kecc(n_providers = 80, provider_size = c(12, 60), rows_per_patient = c(1, 8),
              seed = 12)
pd <- pp_data(d, y = "y", x = c("x1", "x2", "x3"), provider = "provider",
              patient = "patient", message = FALSE)
fit <- fit_logistic_fe(pd)
tst <- test(fit, statistic = "score", variance = "stabilized")
tst
#> Provider tests: score statistic, stabilized variance (modified); null median = -0.9478; two.sided, level 0.95

#>      P005  -1.0141 NA    -0.9478   -0.3859 6.996e-01    0 -1.3498 -0.67883

Every result has the same columns: provider, estimate (the provider effect), se (Wald statistics only), null_value, statistic, p, flag (1 above the null, -1 below, 0 not different, NA not testable), lower, upper. Attributes keep the settings and the provider sizes.

combos <- expand.grid(statistic = c("exact", "score", "wald"),
                      variance = c("naive", "robust", "stabilized"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
combos <- combos[!(combos$statistic == "exact" & combos$variance != "naive"), ]
combos$flagged <- mapply(function(s, v) {
  sum(test(fit, statistic = s, variance = v)$flag != 0, na.rm = TRUE)
}, combos$statistic, combos$variance)
combos
#>   statistic   variance flagged
#> 1     exact      naive      42
#> 2     score      naive      43
#> 3      wald      naive      43
#> 5     score     robust      36
#> 6      wald     robust      42
#> 8     score stabilized      35
#> 9      wald stabilized      40

Arguments:

  • null: "median" (default), "mean" (weighted by rows) or a number.
  • alternative: "two.sided", "greater" (the provider is above the reference) or "less". A measure whose consequential tail is “worse” tests one-sided, at the one-sided level.
  • level: the confidence level; the significance level is 1 - level.
  • providers: a subset to report (every provider still enters the stabilized pooling).
  • exact_method: "poibin" (the Poisson-binomial distribution) or "bootstrap"; n_resample.
  • score_type: "modified" (the other parameters held at their full-model estimates) or "restricted" (re-solved under the null).
  • wald_variance: "case_mix" (default) or "full", see below.
  • statistic = "lr": the likelihood-ratio statistic of one provider effect with the other parameters fixed (ParaFLR), the penalized likelihood for a Firth fit.

The Wald variance

The naive Wald test uses by default the variance of the provider’s fitted average linear predictor, \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\gamma_i + \bar Z_i^\top \hat\beta)\), which does not depend on where the covariates are centred; the "full" variance of \(\hat\gamma_i\) alone does, and with uncentred covariates it changes the flags.

Confidence limits

confint() inverts the chosen test for the provider effects (type = "exact", "score", "wald", "robust_wald"); standardize(level = ) maps those limits to the measures.

head(confint(fit, type = "score"))
#>   provider   estimate      lower      upper
#> 1     P001 -0.3946980 -0.9508951  0.1617724
#> 2     P002 -0.1280870 -0.4455044  0.1893382
#> 3     P003 -0.3444118 -0.7207547  0.0319795
#> 4     P004 -0.6543873 -0.9869470 -0.3217850
#> 5     P005 -1.0141023 -1.2955286 -0.7326444
#> 6     P006 -0.6903412 -1.1846614 -0.1958079

Which test

The rules the measures follow, derived from the data:

  • a provider with all-identical outcomes has no Wald statistic: use the score or the exact statistic (or a Firth fit);
  • with repeated observations per patient the naive variance is wrong: use the robust or the stabilized variance;
  • with few patients per provider the robust variance is unstable: use the stabilized one;
  • when the statistics spread more than \(N(0,1)\) and the spread grows with provider size, calibrate with an empirical null.

The default test(fit) is the exact test; the production choice for a patient-month measure is the robust or stabilized score test (or the robust Wald test on a direct rate) under an empirical null.

Continuous and random-effect models

A linear fit has the score and Wald statistics with the naive (a \(t\) reference with \(n - m - p\) degrees of freedom) or the robust variance; a random-effect fit has the Wald test of the predicted effect.

dc <- sim_kecc(n_providers = 40, type = "continuous", seed = 8)
pc <- pp_data(dc, y = "y", x = c("x1", "x2", "x3"), provider = "provider",
              patient = "patient", message = FALSE)
test(fit_linear_fe(pc), variance = "robust")
#> Provider tests: wald statistic, robust variance; null median = 0.06424; two.sided, level 0.95
#>   40 providers: 15 above, 13 below, 12 not different, 0 not tested
#>  provider estimate      se null_value statistic         p flag    lower   upper
#>      P001  -0.1356 0.13634    0.06424    -1.466 1.427e-01    0 -0.40284  0.1316
#>      P002   0.1761 0.10747    0.06424     1.041 2.978e-01    0 -0.03451  0.3868
#>      P003   0.3824 0.10852    0.06424     2.932 3.370e-03    1  0.16970  0.5951
#>      P004   1.0022 0.14592    0.06424     6.428 1.295e-10    1  0.71618  1.2882
#>      P005  -0.4841 0.09295    0.06424    -5.899 3.654e-09   -1 -0.66630 -0.3019
#>      P006   0.6608 0.11217    0.06424     5.318 1.049e-07    1  0.44093  0.8806
#>   ... 34 more rows

Survival outcomes: tests of the observed-to-expected ratio

For a Cox fit the provider’s measure is \(O_j / E_j\), and test() treats \(O_j\) as Poisson with mean \(E_j\):

  • statistic = "midp" (default): the two-sided mid-p Poisson test turned into a z statistic, whose limits invert the (calibrated) test by root finding, so that a limit excludes 1 exactly when the provider is flagged;
  • "exact": the two-sided Poisson test with the exact chi-square limits (\(E_j < 100\)) or Byar’s approximation; theoretical null only;
  • "wald": \(\log(O_j / E_j) / \sqrt{\phi / O_j}\) with dispersion = "none" (\(\phi = 1\)) or "deviance" (the Poisson deviance of the patient-level counts over its degrees of freedom).

min_expected drops providers with fewer expected events than the measure reports (3, typically) before an empirical null is fitted.

s <- sim_kecc(n_providers = 80, provider_size = c(12, 80), type = "survival", seed = 9)
ps <- pp_data(s, x = c("x1", "x2", "x3"), provider = "provider", patient = "patient",
              time = "stop", start = "start", event = "event", cutoff = 0, message = FALSE)
cox <- fit_cox(ps)
test(cox, min_expected = 3)
#> Provider tests: midp statistic, poisson variance; null ratio = 1; two.sided, level 0.95
#>   80 providers: 14 above, 14 below, 52 not different, 0 not tested
#>  provider estimate se null_value statistic         p flag   lower upper
#>      P001   1.1315 NA          1    0.7526 0.4517142    0 0.80450 1.550

#>      P003   0.4421 NA          1   -1.7871 0.0739269    0 0.14048 1.066

#>      P006   0.3083 NA          1   -1.9199 0.0548665    0 0.05169 1.019

test(cox, statistic = "wald", dispersion = "deviance", min_expected = 3)

Tests of the risk-factor coefficients

summary() tests the coefficients: Wald with the model-based or the patient-clustered robust variance, the likelihood ratio and the score test (refits without the covariate) for the logistic fit; Wald tests of either stage for the Cox fit; plot(summary(fit)) is a forest plot.

summary(fit, test = "robust_wald")
#>   covariate   estimate         se statistic            p      lower      upper
#> 1        x1  0.4951529 0.02386172 20.750933 0.000000e+00  0.4483848  0.5419210
#> 2        x2 -0.4424828 0.04840342 -9.141562 6.155656e-20 -0.5373518 -0.3476139
#> 3        x3  0.2922481 0.02199266 13.288439 0.000000e+00  0.2491433  0.3353530
